Tomato_Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn dark brown with yellow halos. Spots may merge causing leaf blight.
Tomato_Bacterial_spot.cause: Xanthomonas bacteria spread by rain splash and wind.
remedies: Apply copper-based bactericide every 7–10 days
Remove and destroy infected plant material
Avoid overhead irrigation — use drip systems
Rotate crops — do not plant tomatoes in same spot for 2 years
Use certified disease-free seeds

Tomato_Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (target-board pattern). Lower leaves affected first, progressing upward.
Tomato_Early_blight.cause: Alternaria solani fungus. Favors warm, wet weather.
remedies: Apply chlorothalonil or mancozeb fungicide
Remove lower infected leaves immediately
Mulch around plants to prevent soil splash
Ensure proper plant spacing for air circulation
Water at soil level, not on foliage

Tomato_Late_blight.symptoms: Large, greasy, gray-green water-soaked patches. White mold on leaf undersides. Rapid plant collapse in humid conditions.
Tomato_Late_blight.cause: Phytophthora infestans — same pathogen that caused the Irish Potato Famine.
remedies: Apply preventive fungicide (metalaxyl + mancozeb) before disease onset
Remove all infected plants immediately — do not compost
Avoid working in field when plants are wet
Plant resistant varieties (Mountain Magic, Defiant)
Destroy all infected debris at end of season

Tomato_Leaf_Mold.symptoms: Pale green or yellow patches on upper leaf surface. Olive-brown velvety mold on undersides. Leaves curl and wither.
Tomato_Leaf_Mold.cause: Passalora fulva fungus. Thrives in high humidity (>85%) and poor ventilation.
remedies: Improve greenhouse ventilation immediately
Apply copper fungicide or chlorothalonil
Reduce humidity — avoid wetting foliage
Remove affected leaves and destroy
Plant resistant varieties where possible

Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.symptoms: Small circular spots with dark brown borders and light gray/white centers. Tiny black dots (pycnidia) visible in spot centers.
Tomato_Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Septoria lycopersici fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm wet conditions.
remedies: Apply mancozeb or chlorothalonil fungicide
Remove infected lower leaves — bag and discard
Avoid overhead watering
Stake plants to improve airflow
Practice 2-year crop rotation

Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.symptoms: Tiny yellow/bronze stippling on leaves. Fine webbing on undersides. Leaves turn yellow, dry out and fall off.
Tomato_Spider_mites_Two_spotted_spider_m.cause: Tetranychus urticae — a mite, not an insect. Explodes in hot, dry conditions.
remedies: Spray plants with strong jet of water to dislodge mites
Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap every 5–7 days
Use miticide (spiromesifen or bifenazate) for heavy infestations
Introduce predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) for biological control
Keep plants well-watered — drought stresses plants and favors mites

Tomato__Target_Spot.symptoms: Brown lesions with concentric rings forming a target pattern. May affect leaves, stems, and fruit.
Tomato__Target_Spot.cause: Corynespora cassiicola fungus. Thrives in high humidity.
remedies: Apply azoxystrobin or chlorothalonil fungicide
Improve ventilation and reduce canopy density
Remove and destroy all infected plant material
Avoid wetting foliage during irrigation
Scout regularly and treat at first sign

Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.symptoms: Upward curling and yellowing of young leaves. Stunted growth. Flower drop. Infected plants produce little or no fruit.
Tomato__Tomato_YellowLeaf__Curl_Virus.cause: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), transmitted by whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci).
remedies: Control whitefly vector with imidacloprid or thiamethoxam
Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whitefly populations
Install reflective mulch to repel whiteflies
Remove and destroy infected plants immediately to prevent spread
Plant resistant varieties (HM 1823, Shanty) where available

Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.symptoms: Light and dark green mosaic pattern on leaves. Leaves may be distorted, narrow, or fern-like. Fruit may show yellow blotches.
Tomato__Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV). Spread by contact — hands, tools, clothing.
remedies: No cure — remove and destroy infected plants
Disinfect tools with 10% bleach solution between plants
Wash hands thoroughly before handling plants
Control aphids which can spread the virus
Plant certified virus-free seed or resistant varieties

Tomato_healthy.symptoms: No disease symptoms detected. Leaves appear normal green with no spots, lesions, or discoloration.
remedies: Continue regular monitoring every 3–5 days
Maintain balanced fertilization (NPK)
Keep consistent watering schedule
Ensure good airflow between plants
Apply preventive neem oil spray monthly

Potato___Early_blight.symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on older leaves. Yellowing around lesions. Starts on lower foliage.
Potato___Early_blight.cause: Alternaria solani fungus. Favored by alternating wet/dry periods.
remedies: Apply chlorothalonil or mancozeb fungicide preventively
Remove infected lower leaves
Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization
Practice crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Use certified seed potatoes

Potato___Late_blight.symptoms: Water-soaked dark lesions on leaves and stems. White mold on undersides in humid conditions. Tubers develop brown rot.
Potato___Late_blight.cause: Phytophthora infestans. Spreads explosively in cool, wet weather.
remedies: Apply metalaxyl-based fungicide at first sign or forecast
Hill up soil around plants to protect tubers
Destroy all infected plant material — do not compost
Harvest tubers promptly in dry conditions
Plant resistant varieties (Sarpo Mira, Cara)

Potato___healthy.symptoms: No disease symptoms. Healthy green foliage with no lesions or abnormalities.
remedies: Monitor weekly for early signs of blight
Maintain soil moisture consistently
Apply preventive fungicide during wet seasons
Hill soil regularly to protect developing tubers
Scout for aphids and other pests

Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots turning brown with yellow halos. Spots on leaves, stems, and fruit. Defoliation in severe cases.
Pepper__bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Xanthomonas campestris bacteria. Spread by rain, wind, and contaminated tools.
remedies: Apply copper bactericide at weekly intervals
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
Remove heavily infected plants
Avoid working in field after rain
Use disease-free transplants only

Pepper__bell___healthy.symptoms: No disease symptoms. Vibrant green leaves and healthy stem structure.
remedies: Maintain regular inspection schedule
Ensure consistent moisture — peppers hate drought stress
Side-dress with balanced fertilizer at flowering
Control aphids and thrips proactively
Stake plants to prevent stem damage
